name: Fractional Knapsack
use_case: Loading a truck with grain, sand and gravel you can split by weight
description: Sort by value per unit weight and take greedily, splitting the last item to fill the remaining capacity. Greedy works only because items divide.

name: Queue
top_operation: Add to back / remove from front
use_case: Print jobs waiting their turn at a printer
description: FIFO container. O(1) enqueue and dequeue. Used in scheduling and BFS.
code:
from collections import deque

buf = deque()
buf.append(1)       # add to back      O(1)
buf.append(2)
front = buf[0]      # peek             O(1)
buf.popleft()       # remove from front O(1)  -> returns 1

name: Divide and Conquer
use_case: Finding the closest pair of stars by splitting the sky in half
description: Break a problem into independent subproblems, solve each recursively, then combine. The Master Theorem gives the cost.

name: Stack
use_case: The browser back button's history
description: LIFO container. O(1) push and pop. The backbone of recursion, undo, and DFS.
code:

items.append(1)     # push   O(1)
items.append(2)
top = items[-1]     # peek   O(1)
items.pop()         # pop    O(1)  -> returns 2 (last in)

name: Dijkstra
use_case: GPS routing across a road map
description: Shortest paths from a source with non-negative weights. O(E log V) with a binary heap.

name: Fenwick Tree
use_case: Keeping a running total of votes as ballots stream in
description: A compact array where each slot covers a power-of-two block determined by the lowest set bit. Also called a binary indexed tree.

name: Array
use_case: Storing the pixels in one row of an image
description: Contiguous, index-addressable memory. O(1) random access, but O(n) to search or insert in the middle.
code:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 40]
x = arr[2]          # O(1) random access -> 30
arr.append(50)      # amortized O(1)
arr.insert(1, 15)   # O(n): shifts the rest right
del arr[0]          # O(n): shifts the rest left

name: Topological Sort
use_case: Ordering tasks that have prerequisites
description: Linear ordering of a DAG that respects all dependencies. O(V + E) via DFS or Kahn's algorithm.
code:
from collections import deque

def order(graph, indeg):               # graph must be a DAG
    q = deque([u for u in graph if indeg[u] == 0])
    result = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        result.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return result

name: Binary Search
use_case: Looking up a word in a dictionary
description: Halve a sorted range each step. O(log n) time, O(1) space — requires sorted input.

name: 0/1 Knapsack
use_case: Picking items to maximize value under a weight cap
description: Maximize value under a weight cap with a DP table. O(n·W) time and space.

name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
use_case: Listing every prime below a million for a cryptography demo
description: Repeatedly cross out multiples of each surviving number. Everything left standing is prime.

name: Breadth-First Search
use_case: Finding the fewest moves to solve a puzzle
description: Explore a graph level by level with a queue. Finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

name: AVL Tree
use_case: A database index that stays balanced
description: Self-balancing BST that keeps subtree heights within one. Guarantees O(log n) operations.
code:

name: Trie
use_case: Autocomplete suggestions as you type
description: Prefix tree keyed by characters. Lookup is O(k) in the key length, great for autocomplete.

name: Heap
use_case: Always serving the highest-priority task next
description: Complete tree obeying the heap order. O(log n) insert and extract, O(1) peek at the min or max.
code:
a = []

def push(x):                    # O(log n)
    a.append(x)
    i = len(a) - 1
    while i and a[(i - 1) // 2] > a[i]:
        p = (i - 1) // 2
        a[i], a[p] = a[p], a[i]  # sift up
        i = p

smallest = a[0]                 # peek min  O(1)

name: Convex Hull
use_case: Stretching a rubber band around a scatter of pins on a board
description: The smallest enclosing polygon of a point set. Andrew's monotone chain sorts, then keeps only counter-clockwise turns.

name: Graph
use_case: Modeling a social network of friendships
description: Vertices joined by edges. Models networks, maps, and dependencies; stored as lists or a matrix.
code:
adj = {
    "A": ["B", "C"],

neighbors = adj["A"]        # adjacency list -> ["B", "C"]

name: Segment Tree
use_case: The running high score over any slice of a leaderboard
description: A binary structure over an array where each node stores an aggregate of one interval. Range queries and point updates both cost O(log n).
code:
n = len(arr)
t = [0] * (2 * n)
t[n:] = arr
for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
    t[i] = t[2 * i] + t[2 * i + 1]   # build  O(n)

def query(l, r):                     # sum [l, r)   O(log n)
    res = 0
    l += n; r += n
    while l < r:
        if l & 1: res += t[l]; l += 1
        if r & 1: r -= 1; res += t[r]
        l >>= 1; r >>= 1
    return res

name: Floyd-Warshall
use_case: A flight-time table between every pair of airports in a network
description: Considers each vertex in turn as a possible waypoint and relaxes every pair through it. Handles negative weights; no negative cycles.

name: Binary Search Tree
use_case: Keeping a set of keys in sorted order
description: Ordered tree where left < node < right. O(log n) operations when balanced, O(n) when skewed.

name: Tree
use_case: The folder hierarchy on your hard drive
description: A connected acyclic graph with a designated root. Every node has exactly one parent except the root, which has none.

name: Hash Table
use_case: Looking up a username to find its account
description: Maps keys to values via a hash function. O(1) average lookup, O(n) worst case under collisions.
code:
table = {}
table["alice"] = 42      # insert      O(1) avg
value = table["alice"]   # lookup      O(1) avg
exists = "bob" in table  # membership  O(1) avg
del table["alice"]       # delete      O(1) avg

name: Longest Common Subsequence
use_case: Diffing two files or comparing DNA strands
description: Longest subsequence shared by two strings via a 2-D DP table. O(m·n) time and space.

name: Activity Selection
use_case: Booking the most meetings possible into one conference room
description: Sort by finishing time and greedily take each item that starts after the last one taken. Provably optimal by an exchange argument.
code:
spans.sort(key=lambda s: s[1])   # by end time
chosen, last_end = [], float('-inf')

for start, end in spans:
    if start >= last_end:        # no overlap
        chosen.append((start, end))
        last_end = end

name: Minimum Spanning Tree
use_case: Laying the least possible cable to reach every house in a town
description: The cheapest subset of edges that keeps every vertex connected without cycles. Built by Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm.
code:
edges.sort(key=lambda e: e[2])   # (u, v, weight)
picked, total = [], 0

for u, v, w in edges:
    if merge(u, v):              # disjoint-set merge
        picked.append((u, v, w))

name: Longest Increasing Subsequence
use_case: The longest stretch of record-breaking daily temperatures
description: Keeps the smallest possible tail for every achievable length; binary search places each new value. The tails array's length is the answer.

name: Quick Sort
use_case: The default in-memory sort in many libraries
description: Partition around a pivot and recurse. O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst, sorts in place.

name: Linked List
use_case: A music playlist you can splice tracks into
description: Nodes joined by pointers. O(1) insert/remove at a known node, O(n) to search.

name: Union-Find
use_case: Detecting when two walls of a maze already connect
description: A disjoint-set forest with path compression and union by rank. Near-constant amortized cost, bounded by the inverse Ackermann function.
code:
parent = list(range(n))
rank = [0] * n

def rep(x):                     # path compression
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
        x = parent[x]
    return x

def merge(a, b):                # by rank
    ra, rb = rep(a), rep(b)
    if ra == rb: return False
    if rank[ra] < rank[rb]: ra, rb = rb, ra
    parent[rb] = ra
    if rank[ra] == rank[rb]: rank[ra] += 1
    return True

name: Knuth-Morris-Pratt
use_case: Finding a phrase in a document without ever re-reading a character
description: Precomputes a failure table of longest proper prefixes that are also suffixes, so a mismatch never rewinds the text pointer.
code:
def table(p):                    # longest prefix-suffix
    f = [0] * len(p)
    k = 0
    for i in range(1, len(p)):
        while k and p[i] != p[k]:
            k = f[k - 1]
        if p[i] == p[k]:
            k += 1
        f[i] = k
    return f

# text pointer only ever moves forward -> O(n + m)

name: B-Tree
use_case: Indexing a filesystem so each lookup touches only a handful of disk blocks
description: A self-balancing search tree whose nodes hold many sorted keys and children, keeping the height tiny so each level costs one disk read. All leaves sit at the same depth.

name: Deque
use_case: A browser's history list that drops the oldest page once it grows too long
description: Double-ended queue: O(1) insertion and removal at both the front and the back. Works as a stack or a queue, and powers sliding-window algorithms.

name: Red-Black Tree
use_case: The ordered map inside C++'s std::map and Java's TreeMap
description: A self-balancing BST whose nodes are colored red or black. The coloring rules keep the longest path at most twice the shortest, guaranteeing O(log n) operations with few rotations.
code:
RED, BLACK = True, False

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key
        self.color = RED             # new nodes start red
        self.left = self.right = self.parent = None

def rotate_left(root, x):
    y = x.right
    x.right = y.left
    if y.left: y.left.parent = x
    y.parent = x.parent
    if not x.parent: root = y
    elif x is x.parent.left: x.parent.left = y
    else: x.parent.right = y
    y.left, x.parent = x, y
    return root

name: Depth-First Search
use_case: Solving a maze by following one corridor to its dead end before backing up
description: Explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack.

name: Circular Buffer
use_case: Keeping only the last 1,000 log lines in memory, overwriting the oldest
description: A fixed-size array with head and tail indices that wrap around. Constant-time reads and writes with no reallocation; the oldest data is overwritten when it fills up.
code:
class Ring:
    def __init__(self, k):
        self.buf = [None] * k
        self.head = self.size = 0

    def write(self, x):              # O(1), overwrites oldest when full
        tail = (self.head + self.size) % len(self.buf)
        self.buf[tail] = x
        if self.size < len(self.buf):
            self.size += 1
        else:
            self.head = (self.head + 1) % len(self.buf)

    def read(self):                  # O(1), oldest first
        x = self.buf[self.head]
        self.head = (self.head + 1) % len(self.buf)
        self.size -= 1
        return x

name: Bloom Filter
use_case: A browser checking whether a URL might be on a malicious-site list before asking the server
description: A bit array plus k hash functions. Answers 'definitely not present' or 'probably present': false positives are possible, false negatives are not.

name: LRU Cache
use_case: Keeping the most recently viewed product pages in memory and evicting the stalest
description: A hash map plus a doubly linked list. Lookups are O(1), and the least-recently-used entry is evicted once capacity is reached.

name: Skip List
use_case: Redis sorted sets ranking players on a live leaderboard
description: Layers of sorted linked lists where each higher level skips over more elements; a coin flip decides how tall each node is. Expected O(log n) search with simple code.

name: Kruskal's Algorithm
use_case: Laying cable between towns using the cheapest links first, skipping any that would form a loop
description: Greedy minimum-spanning-tree algorithm: sort edges by weight and add each one unless its endpoints are already connected, checked with a disjoint-set.
code:
def cheapest_network(n, edges):
    parent = list(range(n))

    def rep(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    chosen = []
    for w, u, v in sorted(edges):    # O(E log E)
        ru, rv = rep(u), rep(v)
        if ru != rv:                 # skip edges that close a cycle
            parent[ru] = rv
            chosen.append((u, v, w))
    return chosen

name: Monotonic Stack
use_case: Finding, for each day, how many days until a warmer temperature
description: A stack kept in sorted order by popping anything that would break the order. Answers 'next greater/smaller element' for every index in a single O(n) pass.

name: Adjacency Matrix
use_case: Storing a dense flight network where you constantly ask 'is there a direct flight from A to B?'
description: A V×V grid where cell [u][v] holds 1 or the edge weight. Constant-time edge checks at the cost of quadratic space.
code:
INF = float("inf")
grid = [[INF] * V for _ in range(V)]

def connect(u, v, w=1):          # O(1)
    grid[u][v] = w
    grid[v][u] = w

def linked(u, v):                # O(1)
    return grid[u][v] != INF

def neighbors(u):                # O(V), even if u has few edges
    return [v for v in range(V) if grid[u][v] != INF]

name: Merkle Tree
use_case: Letting a phone verify that one transaction belongs to a blockchain block without downloading the block
description: A binary tree where each leaf is the hash of a data block and each parent hashes its two children. One root hash commits to everything; inclusion proofs need only O(log n) sibling hashes.

name: Bitset
use_case: Tracking which of a stadium's 80,000 seats are taken using one bit per seat
description: A packed array of bits, one per element. Set, test and clear are O(1), and whole-set operations like AND/OR handle 64 elements per machine word.

name: Insertion Sort
use_case: Sorting a hand of playing cards as you pick them up one at a time
description: Builds a sorted prefix by sliding each new element left until it fits. Runs in O(n) on nearly sorted input, which is why hybrid sorts use it for small runs.
code:
def arrange(a):
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        x = a[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > x:   # shift bigger items right
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = x
    return a

name: Splay Tree
use_case: A cache where items you looked up recently become faster to find again
description: A self-adjusting BST that rotates every accessed node up to the root. Stores no balance info; operations are amortized O(log n), and recently used keys stay near the top.

name: k-d Tree
use_case: Finding the closest-colored tile for every pixel of a photo mosaic
description: A binary space-partitioning tree over k-dimensional points. Each level splits on the next axis in turn, so nearest-neighbor queries can prune whole half-spaces.

name: Inverted Index
use_case: A search engine finding every page that mentions a word
description: Maps each term to the set of documents (and often positions) that contain it. The core structure behind full-text search engines such as Lucene.

name: Count-Min Sketch
use_case: Spotting the most-requested URLs in a firehose of web traffic using fixed memory
description: A d×w grid of counters with one hash function per row. Estimates how often each item appears in a stream; it can overcount from collisions but never undercounts.

name: Merge Sort
use_case: Sorting a file too big for memory by sorting chunks and then combining them
description: Divide and conquer: split in half, sort each half recursively, then combine the two sorted runs in linear time. Stable, with a guaranteed O(n log n).

name: Gap Buffer
use_case: Typing in Emacs, where nearly every edit lands right where the cursor already is
description: An array with a movable empty gap at the cursor. Typing fills the gap in O(1); moving the cursor shifts text across the gap in O(distance).
code:
class Editor:
    def __init__(self, cap=16):
        self.buf = [""] * cap
        self.lo, self.hi = 0, cap        # empty slots live in [lo, hi)

    def type(self, ch):                  # O(1) at the cursor
        if self.lo == self.hi:
            self._grow()
        self.buf[self.lo] = ch
        self.lo += 1

    def left(self):                      # move cursor: shift one char
        if self.lo:
            self.lo -= 1
            self.hi -= 1
            self.buf[self.hi] = self.buf[self.lo]

    def _grow(self):
        extra = len(self.buf)
        self.buf[self.hi:self.hi] = [""] * extra
        self.hi += extra

name: Separate Chaining
use_case: A contacts app where names that hash to the same slot simply share a short list
description: Hash-table collision resolution where each slot holds a list of every key that hashed there. Average O(1) at a sensible load factor; degrades to O(n) if everything collides.

name: Interval Tree
use_case: Finding every meeting on a calendar that overlaps a proposed time slot
description: A BST keyed on interval start where each node also stores the largest end point in its subtree. That max lets queries skip whole branches that can't overlap.

name: Directed Acyclic Graph
use_case: Git's commit history, where every commit points back to its parent commits
description: A directed graph with no cycles. Every one has a topological order, which makes it the natural model for dependencies, build systems and version histories.

name: Prim's Algorithm
use_case: Wiring a new subdivision by always extending the existing grid with its cheapest next connection
description: Greedy minimum-spanning-tree algorithm that grows one tree from a start vertex, repeatedly adding the lightest edge leaving it, using a priority queue.

name: Treap
use_case: A randomized ordered set in competitive programming that stays balanced without complex rules
description: A BST on keys that is simultaneously a heap on random priorities. The randomness keeps the expected height at O(log n) with short split/join code.
code:
import random

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key, self.pri = key, random.random()
        self.left = self.right = None

def split(t, key):               # -> (keys < key, keys >= key)
    if t is None: return None, None
    if t.key < key:
        t.right, r = split(t.right, key)
        return t, r
    l, t.left = split(t.left, key)
    return l, t

def join(a, b):                  # every key in a < every key in b
    if not a or not b: return a or b
    if a.pri > b.pri:
        a.right = join(a.right, b)
        return a
    b.left = join(a, b.left)
    return b

name: Spatial Hash
use_case: Checking which bullets might hit which enemies in a 2D game without testing every pair
description: Divides space into a uniform grid and hashes each object into its cell, so neighbor queries only check the few surrounding cells.

name: Doubly Linked List
top_operation: Insert / remove at a known node
use_case: A music player's previous-track and next-track buttons
description: Each node points to both the node before and the node after it, so you can walk backward and unlink any node in O(1) given a pointer to it.
code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None

def unlink(node):                # O(1) given the node
    if node.prev: node.prev.next = node.next
    if node.next: node.next.prev = node.prev
    node.prev = node.next = None

def insert_after(node, new):     # O(1)
    new.prev, new.next = node, node.next
    if node.next: node.next.prev = new
    node.next = new

name: Suffix Array
use_case: Searching for any phrase inside an entire genome without rescanning it
description: The sorted list of starting positions of every suffix of a string. Binary search over it finds any substring, and paired with an LCP array it replaces suffix trees in practice.
code:
def build(s):                    # prefix doubling
    n, k = len(s), 1
    rank = [ord(c) for c in s]
    sa = list(range(n))
    while True:
        key = lambda i: (rank[i], rank[i + k] if i + k < n else -1)
        sa.sort(key=key)
        new = [0] * n
        for a, b in zip(sa, sa[1:]):
            new[b] = new[a] + (key(a) != key(b))
        rank = new
        if rank[sa[-1]] == n - 1:
            return sa
        k *= 2

name: Heap Sort
use_case: Sorting on an embedded device with a hard memory cap and no room for a second array
description: Builds a max-heap in place, then repeatedly swaps the maximum to the end and restores the heap. In-place with an O(n log n) worst case, but not stable.

name: Rope
use_case: A text editor inserting characters in the middle of a huge document without shifting everything after them
description: A balanced binary tree whose leaves hold short strings and whose internal nodes store the length of their left side. Concatenation, splitting and mid-text edits run in O(log n).

name: B+ Tree
use_case: A database index answering 'all orders between March and May' by walking along its leaves
description: A B-tree variant where every record lives in the leaves and the leaves are chained in order. Internal nodes hold only routing keys, so a range scan is one descent plus a sequential walk.

name: Linear Probing
use_case: A parking lot where you take the next open spot if yours is taken
description: Open-addressing collision resolution: on a collision, step to the next slot until an empty one turns up. Cache-friendly but prone to clustering, so tables are kept well under full.

name: Sparse Table
top_operation: Range min query (after O(n log n) build)
use_case: Answering millions of 'lowest price between day i and day j' questions on a fixed price history
description: Precomputes the minimum of every power-of-two-length range. Idempotent queries like min/max answer in O(1) by overlapping two blocks; it can't handle updates.

name: Huffman Tree
use_case: Compressing a text file by giving common letters shorter bit codes
description: A binary tree built by repeatedly joining the two least-frequent nodes. Each leaf's root-to-leaf path is an optimal prefix-free code for that symbol.
code:
import heapq
from itertools import count

def build(freqs):
    tick = count()                         # tie-breaker
    pq = [(f, next(tick), sym) for sym, f in freqs.items()]
    heapq.heapify(pq)
    while len(pq) > 1:                     # O(n log n)
        f1, _, a = heapq.heappop(pq)
        f2, _, b = heapq.heappop(pq)
        heapq.heappush(pq, (f1 + f2, next(tick), (a, b)))
    return pq[0][2]

def codes(node, path="", out=None):
    out = {} if out is None else out
    if isinstance(node, tuple):
        codes(node[0], path + "0", out)
        codes(node[1], path + "1", out)
    else:
        out[node] = path or "0"
    return out

name: Binomial Heap
use_case: Combining the job queues of two servers when one of them is shut down
description: A collection of binomial trees, at most one of each order, like the bits of a binary number. Melding two heaps works like binary addition in O(log n).

name: Octree
use_case: Skipping every object outside the camera's view in a 3D game
description: Each node splits its cube into eight smaller cubes, the 3D counterpart of a quadtree. Used in 3D graphics, physics engines and point-cloud processing.

name: Adjacency List
use_case: Storing a social network where most people know only a tiny fraction of everyone
description: Each vertex keeps a list of its neighbors. Space grows with the edges, ideal for sparse graphs; checking a single edge costs O(deg(v)).
code:
from collections import defaultdict

nbrs = defaultdict(list)

def connect(u, v):               # O(1)
    nbrs[u].append(v)
    nbrs[v].append(u)

def linked(u, v):                # O(deg(u))
    return v in nbrs[u]

for v in nbrs["alice"]:          # O(deg) to visit neighbors
    print(v)

name: Radix Tree
use_case: Routing an IP packet by matching the longest prefix of its address
description: A compressed trie where chains of single-child nodes are merged into one edge labeled with a whole substring. Same O(k) lookup, far fewer nodes.

name: In-Order Traversal
use_case: Printing a binary search tree's keys in sorted order
description: Visits the left subtree, then the node itself, then the right subtree. On a BST this yields the keys in sorted order.
code:
def walk(node, out):
    if node is None:
        return out
    walk(node.left, out)
    out.append(node.key)         # between the two children
    walk(node.right, out)
    return out

name: Cuckoo Hash Table
use_case: A network switch that must look up a MAC address in guaranteed constant time
description: Two tables and two hash functions, so every key lives in one of exactly two slots. An insert evicts the occupant to its other slot, making lookups worst-case O(1).

name: Sparse Matrix
use_case: Storing a recommendation matrix of a million users by a million items where almost every cell is zero
description: Stores only the nonzero entries, commonly in compressed sparse row (CSR) form with value, column and row-pointer arrays, so memory and work scale with the nonzeros.

name: Quadtree
use_case: Compressing an image by storing big solid-color areas as a single square
description: Recursively splits a 2D region into four quadrants until each holds little enough data. Used for image compression, collision detection and maps.

name: HyperLogLog
use_case: Counting unique visitors to a website using only a few kilobytes
description: Estimates the number of distinct elements by tracking, per bucket, the longest run of zero bits seen in hashed values. About 2% error using kilobytes of memory.
code:
m = 1024                          # buckets
regs = [0] * m

def add(x):                       # O(1)
    h = hash(x) & ((1 << 64) - 1)
    j = h % m                     # which bucket
    rest = h // m
    rank = 1
    while rest & 1 == 0 and rank < 54:
        rank += 1                 # length of the zero run
        rest >>= 1
    regs[j] = max(regs[j], rank)

def estimate():
    alpha = 0.7213 / (1 + 1.079 / m)
    return alpha * m * m / sum(2.0 ** -r for r in regs)

name: Heapify
use_case: Turning an unsorted list of tasks into a priority queue all at once instead of one insert at a time
description: Builds a binary heap bottom-up by sifting down every internal node from the last one to the root. Total work is O(n), beating n separate O(log n) inserts.

name: Leftist Heap
use_case: An immutable priority queue in a functional programming language
description: A heap-ordered binary tree where every left child's null-path length is at least its sibling's. That keeps the right spine short, so melds take O(log n).
code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, l=None, r=None):
        self.key, self.l, self.r = key, l, r
        self.npl = 1 + min(npl(l), npl(r))

def npl(t): return t.npl if t else 0

def meld(a, b):                  # O(log n) down the right spines
    if not a or not b: return a or b
    if b.key < a.key: a, b = b, a
    l, r = a.l, meld(a.r, b)
    if npl(l) < npl(r): l, r = r, l    # keep the short side on the right
    return Node(a.key, l, r)

name: R-Tree
use_case: A maps app finding every restaurant inside the area currently on screen
description: A balanced tree of nested bounding rectangles, like a B-tree for 2D shapes. Queries descend only into boxes that intersect the search window.

name: Dynamic Array
use_case: A shopping cart that keeps growing as you add items
description: An array that doubles its capacity when full. The occasional O(n) copy averages out to amortized O(1) appends. Python's list and C++'s vector work this way.

name: Fibonacci Heap
use_case: Speeding up Dijkstra's algorithm on huge, dense road networks
description: A lazy collection of heap-ordered trees. Insert, meld and decrease-key are O(1) amortized; extract-min does the cleanup in O(log n).
code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key, self.kids = key, []
        self.parent, self.marked = None, False

roots, best = [], None

def insert(key):                 # O(1): just add a root
    global best
    n = Node(key)
    roots.append(n)
    if best is None or key < best.key:
        best = n
    return n

def decrease_key(n, key):        # O(1) amortized
    global best
    n.key = key
    p = n.parent
    if p and key < p.key:
        cut(n)                   # becomes a new root
        while p.parent and p.marked:
            q = p.parent
            cut(p)               # cascading cut
            p = q
        if p.parent: p.marked = True
    if key < best.key:
        best = n

def cut(n):
    n.parent.kids.remove(n)
    n.parent, n.marked = None, False
    roots.append(n)

name: Ternary Search Tree
use_case: A spell checker's dictionary that needs prefix search with less memory than a 26-way trie
description: A trie whose nodes have three children (less, equal, greater) instead of one per character. Combines BST-like space efficiency with trie-style prefix queries.

name: Min-Max Heap
use_case: A bounded job queue that serves its most urgent job and drops its least urgent from the same structure
description: A complete binary tree whose levels alternate between min-ordering and max-ordering, giving O(1) access to both the smallest and largest elements and O(log n) removal of either.
